chapter_title: Building an FPGA SoC with Qsys and IP Integrator
chapter_summary:
Qsys (now called **Platform Designer** in newer versions of Quartus Prime) is a system design tool that allows you to build complex FPGA SoCs by connecting IP cores through a graphical interface. Instead of writing HDL code to connect a processor to a UART, a memory, and a timer, you use Qsys to drag-and-drop components and connect them with the mouse. Qsys then automatically generates the interconnect logic, address decoding, and HDL files for the entire system.

The Qsys workflow is:
1. Open Qsys from Quartus Prime (**Tools > Platform Designer**).
2. Add a NIOS II processor core to the system canvas.
3. Add on-chip memory (RAM) for the processor's program and data.
4. Add peripherals: UART, timer, GPIO, and any custom components.
5. Connect the components using the Avalon Memory-Mapped bus.
6. Assign base addresses to each peripheral.
7. Generate the system HDL files.
8. Instantiate the generated system in your top-level Quartus Prime project.
9. Write embedded C software for the NIOS II processor.
10. Compile the software and download it to the FPGA along with the hardware bitstream.

The **Avalon Memory-Mapped Interface** is the bus protocol used by Qsys to connect components. It is a simple, synchronous bus with read and write transactions. Each component connected to the bus has a set of signals: `address`, `read`, `write`, `writedata`, `readdata`, and `waitrequest`. The system interconnect fabric (generated by Qsys) acts as an arbiter that routes transactions between the processor (master) and the peripherals (slaves).

When you add a NIOS II processor to Qsys, you configure its parameters:
- **Core type:** Economy, Standard, or Fast.
- **Instruction cache:** Size and line size (for Standard and Fast cores).
- **Data cache:** Size and line size (for Fast core).
- **JTAG debug module:** Enables debugging via the USB-Blaster.
- **Custom instructions:** Allows adding hardware-accelerated operations.

When you add **on-chip memory**, you specify the size (e.g., 64 KB) and the type (RAM or ROM). The on-chip memory is implemented using the FPGA's M9K memory blocks. It is fast and has deterministic access time, but it is limited in size compared to external SDRAM.

When you add a **UART** peripheral, you specify the baud rate, data bits, parity, and stop bits. The UART connects to the NIOS II processor via the Avalon bus and to the external world via FPGA pins (RX and TX).

When you add a **timer** peripheral, you specify the number of timers and their resolution. The timer is used for delay functions, timeouts, and periodic interrupts in the embedded software.

When you add **GPIO** peripherals, you specify the number of input and output bits. GPIO is used for LEDs, switches, and simple digital I/O.

After connecting all components, Qsys generates a system with a unified memory map. Each peripheral is assigned a base address (e.g., UART at 0x00001000, timer at 0x00002000). The processor accesses peripherals by reading from or writing to these addresses. The NIOS II Software Build Tools (SBT) for Eclipse generate C header files with the base addresses and register offsets, so you do not need to hardcode addresses in your software.

The generated system is instantiated in your top-level Verilog or VHDL module:

```verilog
my_qsys_system u0 (
    .clk_clk       (CLK),
    .reset_reset_n (RST_N),
    .uart_0_rxd    (UART_RX),
    .uart_0_txd    (UART_TX),
    .pio_0_export  (LED)
);
```

This instantiation connects the Qsys system's ports to the top-level pins.

screens.title: Building an FPGA SoC with Qsys and IP Integrator
screens.subtitle: Assemble a NIOS II processor, memory, and peripherals through Platform Designer and generate the HDL needed for Quartus Prime integration.

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn a practical, drag-and-drop approach to building an FPGA System on Chip using Qsys, also known as Platform Designer. We focus on assembling a NIOS II processor with on-chip memory, a UART, a timer, and GPIO, then generating the HDL so you can instantiate the whole system in your Quartus Prime project and run embedded software. You will see how the Avalon Memory-Mapped interface standardizes read and write transactions and how the generated interconnect fabric handles address decoding and routing. This approach removes much of the manual HDL plumbing: instead of hand-writing buses and arbiters, you configure cores, assign base addresses, and let Platform Designer produce the glue logic. A concrete use case we return to is a simple Hello, World program that prints over UART and blinks LEDs through an 8-bit GPIO. Along the way we'll discuss common configuration choices for NIOS II cores, the trade-offs for on-chip memory, and what the system interconnect actually does. By the end you'll understand both the visual workflow and the software flow needed to exercise your SoC.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives prepare you to build, configure, and test a simple FPGA SoC using Platform Designer. First, you will learn to add a NIOS II processor, on-chip memory, and peripherals in Qsys and wire them together through the Avalon Memory-Mapped interface. This skill matters because it replaces low-level HDL interconnect wiring with a reliable, generated fabric. Second, you'll understand the Avalon bus signals and how the system interconnect fabric arbitrates transactions and performs address decoding. That understanding helps you reason about latency, waitstates, and peripheral access from software. Third, you will configure the NIOS II core options—core type, caches, and JTAG debug—so your design balances performance and resources. Finally, you will generate the system HDL and integrate it into Quartus Prime so software can run on the hardware. Each objective links to a real task: drag components in Platform Designer, assign base addresses, generate HDL, and run a Hello, World program over UART. Keep these practical goals in mind as we build the system step by step.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on outcomes
keyIdea.text: By the end you'll assemble an SoC visually, generate the interconnect and HDL, configure the processor and peripherals, and run embedded software that uses the memory map.

narration.text: To make these objectives concrete, imagine the lab you'll run: you drag a NIOS II/f core into Platform Designer, add a 64 KB on-chip R A M, one UART set to a common baud rate, a timer, and an 8-bit GPIO for LEDs. You connect the cores via Avalon, assign base addresses, and generate the HDL. In software, you build a Hello, World program that opens the UART and toggles GPIO bits to blink LEDs. This scenario ties each objective to a measurable action: component placement, bus wiring handled by the tool, correct peripheral configuration, and successful software communication. A common misconception is that Platform Designer hides important details; it does not: it generates the interconnect and exposes base addresses and headers that software must use. Understanding the generated memory map and the role of waitrequest and address decoding will help you debug when a peripheral doesn't respond. Keep this lab flow in mind as a repeating example while we unpack each part of the system.

screens.title: What is Qsys / Platform Designer?
screens.subtitle: A visual system integration tool that generates interconnect and HDL

narration.text: Platform Designer, historically called Qsys, is a graphical system-building tool inside Quartus Prime that lets you assemble processors, memories, and peripherals without hand-writing interconnect HDL. The core idea is that IP cores expose Avalon memory-mapped interfaces and the tool automatically creates the system interconnect fabric: address decoding, arbitration, and the glue logic necessary for masters and slaves to communicate. A concrete example is adding a NIOS II processor and a UART: instead of wiring signals manually, you drop both into the canvas, connect their Avalon interfaces, and Platform Designer generates the interconnect and a unified memory map. This both speeds design and reduces human error. A common misconception is that the tool hides low-level details completely. It does not. It exposes the generated signals, base addresses, and header files so you can inspect timings, view waitrequest behavior, and reason about performance. Why this matters: for an embedded project you spend less time on bus plumbing and more on configuring cores, assigning addresses, and writing the software that uses them. Consider: how would your debugging strategy change when the tool provides a generated interconnect versus a hand-coded one?

keyIdea.title: Platform Designer = visual assembly + generated HDL
keyIdea.text: It connects Avalon-enabled IP, generates interconnect logic, and produces the system HDL and a memory map used by embedded software.

content.html:
Definition

Platform Designer explained

Platform Designer is a graphical IP-integrator for FPGA SoCs. It creates the interconnect fabric and a memory map that software uses to access peripherals.

Key role
Auto-generate address decoding, arbitration, and connections between masters and slaves.
Concrete example
Drop NIOS II and UART on the canvas, connect, and generate the HDL and headers used by your C code.
Misconception
Platform Designer doesn't hide signals: it provides generated files and maps so you can debug bus behavior.
Key Takeaway

Use Platform Designer to reduce manual HDL plumbing and speed SoC integration while keeping visibility into generated signals and addresses.

Analogy & Visual
Canvas analogy
Think of the canvas as a schematic: you place functional blocks and the tool wires them into a correct interconnect. This keeps design intent clear and consistent.
Processor
NIOS II core with Avalon master ports
Peripherals
UART, Timer, GPIO as Avalon slaves
Interconnect
Automatically generated fabric and address map
Files
Generated HDL and software headers

screens.title: Qsys / Platform Designer Workflow
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step system assembly from component selection to HDL generation

narration.text: The Qsys workflow follows predictable steps that turn a component canvas into a runnable SoC. First, open Platform Designer from Quartus Prime and populate the canvas with a NIOS II core and any peripherals you need—on-chip memory, UART, timer, and GPIO are common for embedded demos. Second, connect bus interfaces; Platform Designer usually shows compatible ports and can connect masters and slaves automatically. Third, assign base addresses for each peripheral so the processor can access them through a unified memory map. Fourth, configure core parameters: choose NIOS II core type and cache settings, and enable a JTAG debug module if you want source-level debugging. Fifth, generate the system which creates HDL files, a system instantiation template, and software headers that list base addresses and register offsets. Sixth, instantiate the generated system in your top-level Verilog or VHDL module and wire the external pins (UART RX/TX, LED GPIO). Finally, build the embedded C software with the generated headers, program the FPGA with the bitstream and run the software. A common error is skipping address assignment or leaving two peripherals with overlapping ranges; always review the address map before generating HDL. Which step will you double-check first when you build your system?

keyIdea.title: Repeatable workflow
keyIdea.text: Follow a fixed sequence: add cores, configure, connect, assign addresses, generate HDL, integrate, then build software and test.

content.html:
Process

Platform Designer workflow

1. Open Platform Designer
Tools → Platform Designer in Quartus Prime.
2. Add processor and memory
Add a NIOS II core and an on-chip RAM sized for your application, e.g., 64 KB for small demos.
3. Add peripherals and connect
Include UART, timer, and GPIO. Connect via Avalon MM and assign base addresses.
4. Generate system
This step produces HDL, instantiation templates, and C headers with base addresses.
5. Instantiate in top-level design
Use the generated module name and wire its ports to board pins for UART and GPIO.
6. Build embedded software
Use the NIOS II SBT or Eclipse to create a C project that uses generated header files for peripheral addresses.
7. Program and test
Program FPGA, run the program, and verify UART output and GPIO behavior like LED blinking.
Common mistake

Overlapping base addresses cause peripherals not to respond; always review the address map before generation.

screens.title: Avalon Memory-Mapped Interface
screens.subtitle: Signals and transaction behavior used by Platform Designer components

narration.text: The Avalon Memory-Mapped interface is the standard bus protocol that Qsys uses to connect masters and slaves inside a Platform Designer system. It defines a simple synchronous transaction model: masters present an address and either assert read or write along with writedata; slaves respond with readdata and may insert waitrequest cycles to pace transfers. Key signals you will see in generated HDL and in headers are address, read, write, writedata, readdata, and waitrequest. For embedded software, these map to registers at base addresses; for example, writing to a UART transmit register drives bytes out to the serial line. A concrete example: the processor performs a write to the UART's TX register address; the interconnect routes the address, the UART accepts the writedata, and the UART may de-assert waitrequest when it is ready. A misconception to avoid is thinking Avalon enforces a single-cycle response for all slaves. Slaves can use waitrequest to insert stalls, and the interconnect must route and arbitrate multiple masters where present. Understanding this behavior helps you diagnose peripheral stalls and design choices such as using on-chip memory for deterministic access time.

keyIdea.title: Avalon MM fundamentals
keyIdea.text: Address, read/write, writedata, readdata, and waitrequest form the transaction semantics. The interconnect routes and arbitrates these signals between masters and slaves.

content.html:
Definition

Avalon Memory-Mapped Interface

A synchronous bus protocol for read and write transactions between masters and slaves, with optional flow control via waitrequest.

Core signals
  • address: target register or memory location
  • read / write: transaction type
  • writedata / readdata: payload
  • waitrequest: slave-driven flow control
Example
NIOS II writes to UART transmit register; the interconnect routes it and the UART responds when ready, possibly using waitrequest cycles.
Misconception

Avalon does not guarantee single-cycle access; waitrequest lets slaves stall transactions which the interconnect supports.

Transaction flow
Visualizing a typical read transaction helps embed the signals into your mental model.
Read sequence (conceptual)
  1. Master asserts address and read
  2. Interconnect decodes address and routes to slave
  3. Slave may assert waitrequest until data ready
  4. Slave places readdata, deasserts waitrequest
  5. Interconnect returns data to master
Why it matters
Knowing how waitrequest affects timing informs where to place time-critical code and when on-chip memory is preferable for deterministic access.

screens.title: NIOS II Core Configuration Options
screens.subtitle: Choosing Economy, Standard, or Fast and cache/debug trade-offs

narration.text: When adding a NIOS II processor to Platform Designer you must pick a core type and optional features. The three common types are Economy, Standard, and Fast. Economy uses the fewest FPGA resources and is suitable for simple control tasks; it often lacks caches. Standard provides a middle ground and supports an instruction cache for improved program execution speed. Fast is optimized for performance and supports both instruction and optional data caches. You can also enable a JTAG debug module to connect to a USB-Blaster for source-level debugging and set custom instructions for hardware-accelerated operations. A concrete configuration choice: choose Fast with caches if your application has tight loops and memory-heavy processing; choose Economy when resources are limited and code size is small. A frequent misconception is that caches always help; for small on-chip memory with deterministic access, caches may add complexity without benefit. Think about your memory architecture: if code and data fit in fast on-chip R A M, a simple core without caches can be the most predictable choice. Which trade-off matters more in your design: resource usage or raw performance?

keyIdea.title: Pick the right core
keyIdea.text: Economy saves resources, Standard adds instruction caching, Fast adds data caching and higher performance; enable debug when you need step debugging.

content.html:
Comparison

Core types at a glance

Economy
Lowest resource usage; suitable for simple control code; typically no caches.
Standard
Middle ground with instruction cache options to speed code fetches.
Fast
Highest performance, supports instruction and data caches; best for compute-intensive code.
Configuration details
JTAG debug module
Enable to allow source-level debugging using the USB-Blaster. Useful while developing firmware.
Custom instructions
Add hardware-accelerated operations when a computation is a hot spot; adds HDL work to integrate.
Cache trade-offs
Caches increase performance but complicate determinism. If code fits in on-chip RAM, caches may be unnecessary.
Pro tip

Start with Economy or Standard during bring-up. Enable Fast and caches after verifying functional correctness to measure performance gains.

screens.title: On-chip Memory: Size, Type, and Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Why choose on-chip RAM for small embedded programs

narration.text: On-chip memory in an FPGA is implemented using block R A M primitives such as M9K blocks and provides fast, deterministic access times that are ideal for small programs and critical data. When you add on-chip memory in Platform Designer you specify size—64 KB is a common choice for simple Hello, World applications—and type (R A M or ROM). On-chip R A M is limited in capacity compared to external SDRAM but does not require a memory controller or external pins, simplifying the hardware design. A concrete example is storing the program text and small data buffers in on-chip R A M so the processor can execute without waitstates. The trade-off is capacity: for larger applications you must use external memory and a memory controller, which increases pin usage and introduces variable access timing. A common misconception is that bigger off-chip memory is always better; for small embedded demos the predictability of on-chip memory often outweighs its limited size. When designing your SoC, decide what fits on-chip and what needs external memory, and remember that caches can alter that balance if enabled on the NIOS II core.

keyIdea.title: On-chip RAM is fast and deterministic
keyIdea.text: Use on-chip memory for small programs and critical code paths to avoid complex controllers and unpredictable timing.

content.html:
Definition

On-chip memory characteristics

Implemented in FPGA block RAMs, on-chip memory is low-latency and deterministic, ideal for storing code and small datastructures.

Size selection
Choose enough space for code and stack. Example: 64 KB is sufficient for simple embedded demos and Hello, World programs.
Type
RAM for read/write program/data regions; ROM when storing fixed tables or boot code.
Key Takeaway

On-chip memory simplifies design and speeds access, but plan capacity carefully and move large data to external memory when needed.

Practical example
For the lab, configure a 64 KB on-chip RAM to hold program code and small data structures. This allows deterministic execution and easy bring-up without an external controller.
Why not always use external SDRAM?
External memory needs a controller, pins, and may introduce variable latency and waitstates. It is necessary for large applications but overkill for tiny demos.
Benefit
Deterministic access time
Limitation
Limited capacity vs external SDRAM

screens.title: Configuring UART, Timer, and GPIO Peripherals
screens.subtitle: Parameter choices and software implications for common IP cores

narration.text: Peripherals like UART, timer, and GPIO are configured in Platform Designer with parameters that directly affect software behavior. For UART you set baud rate, data bits, parity, and stop bits; the software opens the serial device at that baud rate and writes bytes to the transmit register. For the lab example, 115200 baud is a common, reliable default for terminals. Timers allow periodic interrupts and delays; you configure the number of timers and their resolution for timekeeping or scheduling tasks in your firmware. GPIO peripherals define input and output widths; an 8-bit GPIO can drive eight LEDs and the software toggles its output register to blink them. Important: the Avalon memory map assigns each peripheral a base address and register offsets, so software writes to generated header constants rather than hard-coded addresses. A common mistake is mismatching UART settings between the board and terminal, which causes garbled output. Another is assuming a timer will generate interrupts without enabling them in software. Always cross-check peripheral parameters and generated register names in the headers before compiling your firmware. Configuring UART, Timer, and GPIO Peripherals means choose uart parameters, timer resolution, and gpio widths deliberately and use generated headers to access registers in software.. In practical terms, parameter choices and software implications for common ip cores. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Peripheral configuration matters
keyIdea.text: Choose UART parameters, timer resolution, and GPIO widths deliberately and use generated headers to access registers in software.

content.html:
Peripherals

UART, Timer, GPIO settings

UART
Set baud (e.g., 115200), data bits, parity, and stop bits. Software writes transmit bytes to the TX register defined by the base address.
Timer
Choose number of timers and resolution; timers are used for delays, timeouts, and periodic interrupts that the software handles.
GPIO
Specify input/output bit width. Example: an 8-bit output drives eight LEDs; toggle bits to blink LEDs from firmware.
Software implication
Use generated header constants for base addresses and offsets to access peripheral registers. This avoids hard-coded addresses and eases portability.
Concrete example
Configure UART at 115200, add an 8-bit GPIO for LEDs, and a timer with a 1 ms resolution for blinking logic in firmware.
Common mistake

Mismatched UART settings between firmware and terminal produce unreadable output; verify baud and parity on both ends.

screens.title: System Interconnect Fabric and Address Decoding
screens.subtitle: How the generated fabric routes transactions and assigns base addresses

narration.text: The system interconnect fabric generated by Platform Designer is the glue that connects masters like the NIOS II processor to slaves such as UART, timer, and GPIO. It performs two critical jobs: address decoding and arbitration. Address decoding maps each incoming address to the correct peripheral based on the base addresses you assign; arbitration resolves simultaneous access when multiple masters exist. The fabric also handles waitrequest propagation during slow peripheral accesses. In practice you assign base addresses—for example, UART at 0x00001000 and timer at 0x00002000—so software reads and writes known addresses. Platform Designer displays the memory map after you place and connect peripherals; review it to avoid overlaps. A concrete scenario: if two peripherals share overlapping address ranges, a read may route to the wrong device or be ignored, leading to hard-to-find bugs. Another important point is that the interconnect is synthesized into HDL and becomes part of the design's timing closure considerations. Understanding the role of the fabric helps you interpret bus traces, debug peripheral non-responsiveness, and reason about the performance impact of waitstates in your system. System Interconnect Fabric and Address Decoding means the generated fabric decodes addresses, routes transactions, arbitrates access, and propagates waitrequest signals between masters and slaves.. In practical terms, how the generated fabric routes transactions and assigns base addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interconnect responsibilities
keyIdea.text: The generated fabric decodes addresses, routes transactions, arbitrates access, and propagates waitrequest signals between masters and slaves.

content.html:
Architecture

Interconnect fabric roles

Address decoding
Routes each address to its peripheral using the base address and offsets you assigned in Platform Designer.
Arbitration
If multiple masters exist, the fabric decides which master accesses a slave at a time to avoid bus conflicts.
Flow control
Waitrequest is passed to masters when a slave needs to stall, ensuring correct timing across devices.
Memory map example
Platform Designer generates a unified address map; typical assignments might place UART at 0x00001000 and timer at 0x00002000. Confirm these values in the GUI and generated headers.
Troubleshooting tip
If a peripheral doesn't respond, check for address overlap and inspect waitrequest behavior in the generated HDL or with simulation tools.
Reflective question

How will you validate that each peripheral's base address is unique and correct before generating HDL?

screens.title: Generated HDL and Top-level Instantiation
screens.subtitle: Using the generated module in your Quartus Prime design

narration.text: After you generate the system in Platform Designer, the tool emits HDL files and a suggested instantiation template that you include in your Quartus Prime top-level design. The generated module typically has named ports for clocks, resets, and external signals like UART RX/TX and GPIO lines. For example, a generated instantiation looks like a module named my_qsys_system with ports named clk_clk, reset_reset_n, uart_0_rxd, uart_0_txd, and pio_0_export. In Verilog you instantiate that module and connect its ports to your board-level signals. This step maps the SoC's external interfaces to FPGA pins and prepares the design for synthesis and place-and-route. A common misconception is that generation is the final step; you must still integrate and compile the top-level project and ensure pin assignments match the board. Also examine the generated HDL if you need to understand timing paths or include constraints. Finally, regenerate the system when you change parameterization or peripheral selection so generated headers and HDL remain consistent with your software and top-level design. Generated HDL and Top-level Instantiation means include the generated system module in your top-level verilog/vhdl and wire its external ports to board pins for uart and gpio testing.. In practical terms, using the generated module in your quartus prime design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiate and pin out
keyIdea.text: Include the generated system module in your top-level Verilog/VHDL and wire its external ports to board pins for UART and GPIO testing.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Generated instantiation example

<!-- Verilog instantiation example from Platform Designer -->
my_qsys_system u0 (
    .clk_clk       (CLK),
    .reset_reset_n (RST_N),
    .uart_0_rxd    (UART_RX),
    .uart_0_txd    (UART_TX),
    .pio_0_export  (LED)
);
The generated module name and port names come from the system's settings. Replace the uppercase signals with your board's actual pin nets and add pin assignments in the Quartus assignments editor.
Integration checklist
  • Instantiate the generated module in your top-level file.
  • Map UART and GPIO ports to board pins and update pin constraints.
  • Regenerate system after parameter changes and rebuild the project.
Why check generated HDL?
Inspect it for timing-critical paths, or to understand how the interconnect handles waitrequest and arbitration.
Key Takeaway

Instantiation bridges the generated system to board pins; always align pin assignments and regenerate when the system changes.

screens.title: Software Flow: Generated Headers and Hello, World
screens.subtitle: Using the NIOS II SBT and generated register definitions in C

narration.text: Once the system is generated and instantiated, Platform Designer emits C header files that define peripheral base addresses and register offsets. Use the NIOS II Software Build Tools (SBT) for Eclipse to create a C project that includes these generated headers; they remove the need to hard-code addresses. A typical Hello, World program opens the UART device and writes a string to its transmit register while toggling GPIO outputs to blink LEDs on a timer tick. For the hands-on activity, include the generated header and call the provided macros or constants that map register names to addresses. A common misconception is that you must guess addresses; the generated headers are authoritative and portable across rebuilds so long as you re-generate them after hardware changes. Also remember to compile the software after generating the system so the headers match the hardware. When testing, open a terminal at the configured UART baud rate and confirm that the Hello, World message appears and LEDs blink, which verifies both hardware wiring and software register accesses. Software Flow: Generated Headers and Hello, World means use the software headers produced by platform designer in your c projects so code addresses match the hardware memory map automatically.. Process

Software build and example

Include the generated header with base address constants and use them to access peripheral registers in C. The SBT for Eclipse integrates these headers into your project automatically.
Example snippet (conceptual)
/* Pseudocode using generated base address macros */
#define UART_BASE 0x00001000
#define UART_TX   (UART_BASE + 0x00)
#define GPIO_BASE 0x00003000

/* Send a character */

/* Toggle LEDs */
*((volatile unsigned int *)GPIO_BASE) ^= 0x01;
Use real generated macros from the Platform Designer headers in your project rather than these placeholders.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Build and Test the Simple SoC
screens.subtitle: Step sequence for the Hello, World and LED blink lab

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through a complete flow: build a Platform Designer system, generate HDL, integrate it into your Quartus Prime project, and write firmware to print over UART and blink LEDs. Start by creating a new Platform Designer system and add a NIOS II/f core, a 64 KB on-chip R A M, a UART configured to 115200 baud, a timer, and an 8-bit GPIO output. Connect all Avalon interfaces and ensure the processor's data and instruction masters are wired to the interconnect. Assign base addresses, for example UART at 0x00001000 and GPIO at 0x00003000, then generate the system. Instantiate the generated module in your top-level Verilog and map UART pins to your board's USB-to-UART bridge and GPIO to the LEDs. Regenerate the system if you change parameters. In software, create a NIOS II project in SBT for Eclipse, include the generated header, and write a program that prints a Hello, World string to UART and toggles a GPIO bit on timer interrupts or delays. Program the FPGA, open a terminal at 115200 baud, and verify the text appears and the LEDs blink. A common failure point is forgetting to assign pins or mismatched UART settings; double-check both if the test fails.

narration.text: These are the core concepts to carry forward. Platform Designer (Qsys) enables visual SoC assembly and generates the interconnect fabric and HDL. The Avalon Memory-Mapped interface defines transactions using address, read/write, data, and waitrequest signals—understanding these helps you debug timing and stalls. Configure the NIOS II core based on resource and performance needs, and enable JTAG debug when you require source-level stepping. Use on-chip memory for small, deterministic programs, and configure UART, timer, and GPIO peripherals with matching parameters in software. Finally, always review the generated memory map and headers before building firmware, and instantiate the generated system properly in your top-level design. Keep these points in mind as you build and iterate: they connect the graphical workflow to the runtime behavior you observe on the board. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you start the lab

narration.text: Keep this quick checklist at hand when you build your SoC: verify the memory map and base addresses to avoid overlaps; ensure UART and GPIO pins are assigned correctly on the top-level design and match terminal settings; and regenerate Platform Designer outputs whenever you change cores or peripheral parameters so headers and HDL stay in sync. These minutes of validation prevent the most common failures during hardware-software bring-up. When you program the FPGA and the UART doesn't print or LEDs don't blink, revisit this checklist systematically: addresses, pins, and regenerated headers. This practice turns ambiguous failures into diagnosable steps and shortens debug time during board bring-up.
